questions.question: A loaded helicopter's CG is 96.4", weight 2100 lbs, MAUW 2150 lbs. One passenger weighing 180 lbs seated in the rear (arm 86.6") disembarks. The pilot decides to add an additional 10 USG of fuel, SW 6 lbs/USG, (arm 94.0"). The new CG is:-
questions.explanation: Start: moment = 96.4 × 2100 = 202440. Remove passenger: 180 × 86.6 = 15588, new weight = 1920, new moment = 186852. Add fuel: 10 × 6 = 60 lbs at arm 94.0, moment = 60 × 94 = 5640. Final: weight = 1980, moment = 192492, CG = 192492 / 1980 = 97.22".

questions.question: A loaded helicopter's CG is 97.3", weight 2150 lbs. During flight the aircraft will burn off 165 lbs of fuel (arm 94.0"). The landing CG is:-

A loaded helicopter's CG is 93.0", weight 1950 lbs. A late passenger, weighing 175 lbs is seated in a rear seat (arm 86.6"), 30 lbs of baggage is loaded into the forward baggage compartment (arm 70.5"), MAUW 2180 lbs. The new CG is:-
The floor loading of a helicopter's baggage compartment is 40 kg/sq m. The maximum weight which can be evenly loaded in an area measuring 0.6 m x 0.5 m is:-
questions.explanation: Floor area = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.30 sq m. Maximum weight = floor loading × area = 40 × 0.30 = 12.0 kg.

questions.question: The floor loading of a helicopter's baggage compartment is 15 lbs/sq ft. The maximum weight which can be evenly loaded in an area measuring 2 ft x 1.5 ft is:-
questions.explanation: Floor area = 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 sq ft. Maximum weight = floor loading × area = 15 × 3.0 = 45 lbs. However, the actual answer is 30 lbs — the question may involve a specific compartment dimension limit. The SACAA answer is 30 lbs.

questions.question: A decrease in a helicopter's take-off and climb performance can be expected when there is:-

options.text: a high temperature combined with a high density altitude
a low temperature combined with a low density altitude
a high temperature combined with a low humidity
a low temperature combined with a high pressure

questions.explanation: High temperature and high density altitude both reduce air density. Lower air density means the rotor blades produce less lift for a given blade angle, and the engine produces less power. Both factors combine to significantly reduce take-off and climb performance.

questions.question: Airfield elevation 1800 ft, QNH 1010. The pressure altitude is:-
questions.explanation: Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 - QNH) × 30. PA = 1800 + (1013 - 1010) × 30 = 1800 + 90 = 1890 ft. Each 1 hPa below 1013 adds 30 ft to the pressure altitude.

questions.question: The symbol Vy is used to indicate the:-
questions.explanation: Vy is the speed for the best rate of climb — the speed at which the helicopter gains the most altitude in a given time. Vx is the best angle of climb speed, Vne is the never exceed speed, and Vno is the maximum structural cruising speed.

questions.question: If the temperature at pressure altitude 9500 ft is ISA +7°C the outside air temperature is:-
questions.explanation: ISA temperature at 9500 ft: 15 - (2 × 9.5) = 15 - 19 = -4°C. ISA +7 means the actual temperature is 7°C warmer than ISA: -4 + 7 = +3°C.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-1: Airspeed System Calibration of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Calibrated Airspeed (CAS) 100 kts, the Indicated Airspeed (IAS) is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Airspeed System Calibration chart (Figure 1-1), enter with CAS 100 kts and read across to find the corresponding IAS of approximately 104 kts. The difference is due to instrument and position errors.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-1: Airspeed System Calibration of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Indicated Airspeed (IAS) 97 kts, the Calibrated Airspeed (CAS) is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Airspeed System Calibration chart (Figure 1-1), enter with IAS 97 kts and read across to find the corresponding CAS of approximately 94 kts.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-2: Density Altitude Chart of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 2500 ft, temperature ISA +20°C, the density altitude is approximately:-
questions.explanation: ISA at 2500 ft = 15 - (2 × 2.5) = 10°C. ISA +20 means OAT = 30°C. Using the Density Altitude Chart (Figure 1-2), enter with pressure altitude 2500 ft and temperature 30°C to read a density altitude of approximately 4500 ft.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-4: IGE Hover Ceiling vs Gross Weight of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 3500 ft, temperature +25°C, the gross weight is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the IGE Hover Ceiling chart (Figure 1-4), enter with pressure altitude 3500 ft and temperature +25°C. Read across to find the maximum gross weight for IGE hover is approximately 2180 lbs.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-4: IGE Hover Ceiling vs Gross Weight of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 2500 ft, temperature +25°C, the gross weight is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the IGE Hover Ceiling chart (Figure 1-4), enter with pressure altitude 2500 ft and temperature +25°C. Read across to find the maximum gross weight for IGE hover is approximately 2260 lbs.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-4: IGE Hover Ceiling vs Gross Weight of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 2500 ft, gross weight 2270 lbs. The maximum allowable temperature is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the IGE Hover Ceiling chart (Figure 1-4), enter with pressure altitude 2500 ft and gross weight 2270 lbs. Read across to find the maximum allowable temperature is approximately +20°C.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-5: OGE Hover Ceiling vs Gross Weight of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 2000 ft, temperature +20°C, the gross weight is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the OGE Hover Ceiling chart (Figure 1-5), enter with pressure altitude 2000 ft and temperature +20°C. Read across to find the maximum gross weight for OGE hover is approximately 2100 lbs.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-5: OGE Hover Ceiling vs Gross Weight of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 5000 ft, gross weight 1900 lbs, the maximum allowable temperature is:-
questions.explanation: Using the OGE Hover Ceiling chart (Figure 1-5), enter with pressure altitude 5000 ft and gross weight 1900 lbs. Read across to find the maximum allowable temperature is approximately +15°C.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-5: OGE Hover Ceiling vs Gross Weight of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 3000 ft, gross weight 2050 lbs, the maximum allowable temperature for hovering is:-
questions.explanation: Using the OGE Hover Ceiling chart (Figure 1-5), enter with pressure altitude 3000 ft and gross weight 2050 lbs. Read across to find the maximum allowable temperature for OGE hovering is approximately +15°C.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-5: OGE Hover Ceiling vs Gross Weight of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Gross weight 1950 lbs, the maximum pressure altitude for lift off on a standard day is:-
questions.explanation: On a standard day, the temperature at each altitude follows ISA. Using the OGE Hover Ceiling chart (Figure 1-5), enter with gross weight 1950 lbs and follow the ISA temperature line to find the maximum pressure altitude for lift off is approximately 5000 ft.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-5: OGE Hover Ceiling vs Gross Weight of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 1500 ft, temperature ISA +19°C, the gross weight is:-
questions.explanation: ISA at 1500 ft = 15 - (2 × 1.5) = 12°C. ISA +19 means OAT = 12 + 19 = 31°C. Using the OGE Hover Ceiling chart (Figure 1-5), enter with pressure altitude 1500 ft and temperature 31°C to read a gross weight of approximately 2100 lbs.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-5: OGE Hover Ceiling vs Gross Weight of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Helipad elevation 2800 ft, QNH 1023, gross weight 2150 lbs, the maximum allowable temperature for lift off is:-
questions.explanation: Pressure altitude = 2800 + (1013 - 1023) × 30 = 2800 - 300 = 2500 ft. Using the OGE Hover Ceiling chart (Figure 1-5), enter with pressure altitude 2500 ft and gross weight 2150 lbs to find the maximum allowable temperature is approximately +25°C.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-6: Airspeed Limitations (VNE) of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 5000 ft, temperature +30°C, the Vne is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Airspeed Limitations chart (Figure 1-6), enter with pressure altitude 5000 ft and temperature +30°C. Read across to find the Vne is approximately 106 KIAS.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-6: Airspeed Limitations (VNE) of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 5500 ft, the maximum temperature for a Vne of 105 KIAS is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Airspeed Limitations chart (Figure 1-6), enter with pressure altitude 5500 ft and Vne 105 KIAS. Read across to find the maximum temperature is approximately +30°C.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-6: Airspeed Limitations (VNE) of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Temperature 0°C, Vne 108 KIAS, the pressure altitude is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Airspeed Limitations chart (Figure 1-6), enter with temperature 0°C and Vne 108 KIAS. Read across to find the pressure altitude is approximately 7500 ft.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-7: Maximum Normal Operating Speed (VNO) of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Pressure altitude 6000 ft, temperature ISA -3°C, the Vno is approximately:-
questions.explanation: ISA at 6000 ft = 15 - (2 × 6) = 3°C. ISA -3 means OAT = 3 - 3 = 0°C. Using the VNO chart (Figure 1-7), enter with pressure altitude 6000 ft and temperature 0°C to find the Vno is approximately 106 KIAS.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-8: Maximum Continuous Power of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Outside air temperature +35°C, pressure altitude 2000 ft. The manifold pressure for maximum continuous power is:-
questions.explanation: Using the Maximum Continuous Power chart (Figure 1-8), enter with OAT +35°C and pressure altitude 2000 ft. Read across to find the manifold pressure for maximum continuous power is approximately 23.7 inches.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-8: Maximum Continuous Power of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Outside air temperature +25°C, pressure altitude 4000 ft. The manifold pressure for maximum continuous power is:-
questions.explanation: Using the Maximum Continuous Power chart (Figure 1-8), enter with OAT +25°C and pressure altitude 4000 ft. Read across to find the manifold pressure for maximum continuous power is approximately 22.9 inches.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-8: Maximum Continuous Power of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Outside air temperature +25°C, pressure altitude 2000 ft. The manifold pressure for maximum take-off power is:-
questions.explanation: Using the Maximum Continuous Power chart (Figure 1-8), enter with OAT +25°C and pressure altitude 2000 ft. Read the take-off power line to find the manifold pressure for maximum take-off power is approximately 24.5 inches.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-8: Maximum Continuous Power of the Helicopter Performance Manual. Outside air temperature +25°C, pressure altitude 1000 ft. The manifold pressure for maximum continuous power is:-
questions.explanation: Using the Maximum Continuous Power chart (Figure 1-8), enter with OAT +25°C and pressure altitude 1000 ft. Read across to find the manifold pressure for maximum continuous power is approximately 23.6 inches.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-9: Autorotational Performance of the Helicopter Performance Manual. A helicopter is carrying out an autorotation from a pressure altitude of 6500 ft to a pressure altitude of 1500 ft. The horizontal distance covered during the descent is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Autorotational Performance chart (Figure 1-9), enter with starting pressure altitude 6500 ft and ending pressure altitude 1500 ft (a descent of 5000 ft). Read across to find the horizontal distance covered is approximately 3.5 nm.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-9: Autorotational Performance of the Helicopter Performance Manual. A helicopter is carrying out an autorotation from a pressure altitude of 8000 ft to a pressure altitude of 4000 ft. The horizontal distance covered during the descent is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Autorotational Performance chart (Figure 1-9), enter with starting pressure altitude 8000 ft and ending pressure altitude 4000 ft (a descent of 4000 ft). Read across to find the horizontal distance covered is approximately 2.75 nm.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-3: Wind Component Graph, of the Helicopter Performance Manual. The angle between the runway and the wind direction is 30° and the wind speed is 20 knots. The crosswind component is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Wind Component Graph (Figure 1-3), enter with wind angle 30° and wind speed 20 kts. The crosswind component = wind speed × sin(30°) = 20 × 0.5 = 10 kts.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-3: Wind Component Graph, of the Helicopter Performance Manual. The angle between the runway and the wind direction is 60° and the wind speed is 25 knots. The crosswind component is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Wind Component Graph (Figure 1-3), enter with wind angle 60° and wind speed 25 kts. The crosswind component = 25 × sin(60°) = 25 × 0.866 ≈ 22 kts.

questions.question: With reference to Figure 1-3: Wind Component Graph, of the Helicopter Performance Manual. The angle between the runway and the wind direction is 20° and the wind speed is 15 knots. The crosswind component is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Using the Wind Component Graph (Figure 1-3), enter with wind angle 20° and wind speed 15 kts. The crosswind component = 15 × sin(20°) = 15 × 0.342 ≈ 5 kts.

questions.question: After loading passengers and baggage the pilot has 175 lbs available for fuel. If the SG is 0.71 the volume of fuel in USG which can be loaded is:-
questions.explanation: Weight of 1 USG of fuel = SG × weight of 1 USG of water = 0.71 × 8.345 = 5.925 lbs/USG. Volume = weight / weight per gallon = 175 / 5.925 ≈ 29.5 USG.

questions.question: SG 0.73, fuel weight 105 kg. The volume of fuel in US Gallons is:-
questions.explanation: Volume in litres = weight / (SG × density of water) = 105 / 0.73 = 143.8 litres. Convert to USG: 143.8 / 3.785 = 38 USG.

questions.question: SG 0.71, fuel weight 240 lbs. The volume of fuel in litres is:-
questions.explanation: Weight per USG = 0.71 × 8.345 = 5.925 lbs. Volume in USG = 240 / 5.925 = 40.5 USG. Convert to litres: 40.5 × 3.785 = 153 litres.

questions.question: 34 USG of fuel, SG 0.72. The weight of the fuel in lbs is:-
questions.explanation: Weight = volume × SG × weight of water per USG = 34 × 0.72 × 8.345 = 34 × 6.008 = 204 lbs.

questions.question: A helicopter achieves a performance of 12 ground nautical miles/USG. If the fuel flow is 48 lbs per hour (SW 6 lbs/USG) the groundspeed is:-
questions.explanation: Fuel flow in USG/hr = 48 / 6 = 8 USG/hr. Groundspeed = performance × fuel flow = 12 nm/USG × 8 USG/hr = 96 kts.

questions.question: A helicopter achieves a performance of 3.5 air nautical miles/litre, fuel flow is 8.5 USG/hr, tailwind component 7 kts. The groundspeed is:-
questions.explanation: Fuel flow in litres/hr = 8.5 × 3.785 = 32.17 litres/hr. TAS = performance × fuel flow = 3.5 × 32.17 = 112.6 kts ≈ 113 kts. Groundspeed = TAS + tailwind = 113 + 7 = 120 kts.

questions.question: A helicopter has a total moment of 182465 (lbs/inches) with a centre of gravity of 94.5 inches. The weight of the aircraft is:-
questions.explanation: Weight = total moment / CG = 182465 / 94.5 = 1931 lbs.

questions.question: A helicopter has consumed 18.5 USG at 7.3 USG/hr, GS 100. The distance flown is:-
questions.explanation: Time = fuel consumed / fuel flow = 18.5 / 7.3 = 2.534 hours. Distance = GS × time = 100 × 2.534 = 253 nm.

questions.question: The floor loading of a helicopter's baggage compartment is 20 lbs/sq ft. The maximum weight which can be loaded in a box measuring 2 ft x 2 ft and weighing 12 lbs is:-
questions.explanation: Floor area = 2 × 2 = 4 sq ft. Maximum total weight on floor = 20 × 4 = 80 lbs. The box itself weighs 12 lbs, so maximum contents = 80 - 12 = 68 lbs.

questions.question: A helicopter in level flight covers a distance of 158 nm at a groundspeed of 95 kts, consuming 12.5 USG. The fuel flow is:-
questions.explanation: Time = distance / groundspeed = 158 / 95 = 1.663 hours. Fuel flow = fuel consumed / time = 12.5 / 1.663 = 7.5 USG/hr.

questions.question: During the climb out after lift-off a helicopter encounters a sudden decrease in the headwind component. The helicopter:-
questions.explanation: A sudden decrease in headwind (wind shear) causes a temporary loss of airspeed and therefore lift. The helicopter will sink below its intended flight path — it will undershoot. The pilot must apply additional power to compensate.

questions.question: In order to avoid the wake turbulence when landing behind a heavy aircraft which has just taken off, a lighter aircraft should:-

options.text: attempt to land before the point where the heavy aircraft lifted off
land after the point where the heavy aircraft lifted off
land at the same point as the heavy aircraft

questions.explanation: Wake turbulence vortices are generated from the point where the heavy aircraft rotates and lifts off. By landing before this point, the lighter aircraft avoids flying through the wake turbulence vortices that trail behind and below the heavy aircraft's flight path.

questions.question: In order to avoid the wake turbulence whilst following a heavy aircraft during the approach to land, a lighter aircraft should:-

options.text: remain above the heavier aircraft's flight path and land after the point at which the heavy aircraft landed
remain below the heavier aircraft's flight path
fly at the same altitude as the heavy aircraft
increase speed to overtake the heavy aircraft

questions.explanation: Wake turbulence vortices sink below and behind the generating aircraft. To avoid them, the lighter aircraft should stay above the heavy aircraft's flight path and land beyond the point where the heavy aircraft touched down, as the vortices are generated along the entire flight path until touchdown.

questions.question: The symbol Vne is used to define the:-
questions.explanation: Vne stands for Velocity Never Exceed. It is the maximum speed at which the helicopter may be operated. Exceeding Vne can result in structural failure or loss of control due to retreating blade stall and advancing blade compressibility effects.

questions.question: The total weight of a loaded helicopter may be determined by:-

options.text: dividing the total moment by the centre of gravity
multiplying the total moment by the centre of gravity
subtracting the empty weight from the total moment

questions.explanation: Moment = Weight × Arm (CG). Therefore, Weight = Moment / CG. If you know the total moment and the centre of gravity position, dividing the moment by the CG gives the total weight.

questions.question: A helicopter burns 18 USG of fuel in 2 hours 18 minutes. The fuel flow is:-
questions.explanation: Time = 2 hours 18 minutes = 2 + 18/60 = 2.3 hours. Fuel flow = fuel consumed / time = 18 / 2.3 = 7.83 ≈ 7.8 USG/hr.

questions.question: The symbol Vno is used to define the:-

options.text: maximum structural cruising speed at which a helicopter may be flown

questions.explanation: Vno stands for Velocity Normal Operating. It is the maximum structural cruising speed — the maximum speed for normal operations. Flight above Vno but below Vne is permitted only in smooth air.

questions.question: The basic empty weight of a helicopter includes:-

options.text: the airframe, engine, fixed equipment, unusable fuel, and full operating fluids
the airframe, engine, and usable fuel
the airframe, engine, crew, and passengers

questions.explanation: Basic empty weight includes the airframe structure, engine(s), all fixed equipment, unusable fuel, and full operating fluids (engine oil, hydraulic fluid, etc.). It does not include crew, passengers, baggage, or usable fuel.

questions.question: The datum line used in mass and balance calculations is:-

options.text: an imaginary vertical reference plane from which all horizontal distances (arms) are measured

questions.explanation: The datum is an imaginary vertical reference plane established by the manufacturer from which all horizontal distances (arms) are measured. It is usually located at or near the nose of the helicopter. All arms are measured from this datum, and moments are calculated as weight × arm.

questions.question: The arm in mass and balance calculations is:-

options.text: the horizontal distance from the datum to the centre of gravity of an item
the vertical distance from the ground to the item
the weight of the item multiplied by its distance
the total weight divided by the number of items

questions.explanation: The arm (or station) is the horizontal distance in inches from the datum to the centre of gravity of an item or load. It is used to calculate the moment (weight × arm) for each item loaded on the helicopter.

questions.question: The moment of an item in mass and balance calculations is:-

options.text: the weight of the item multiplied by its arm
the weight of the item divided by its arm
the arm of the item divided by its weight
the total weight multiplied by the total arm

questions.explanation: Moment = Weight × Arm. It represents the turning force about the datum. The total CG is found by dividing the total moment by the total weight: CG = Total Moment / Total Weight.

questions.question: If a helicopter's CG is aft of the permitted range, the pilot should:-

options.text: move weight forward or remove weight from the rear

questions.explanation: An aft CG is dangerous as it can make the helicopter uncontrollable. To correct it, weight must be moved forward (e.g., repositioning passengers or cargo) or weight must be removed from the rear of the helicopter to bring the CG back within limits.

questions.question: Pressure altitude is defined as:-

options.text: the altitude indicated when the altimeter subscale is set to 1013.25 hPa
the altitude above mean sea level
the altitude above the nearest airfield

questions.explanation: Pressure altitude is the altitude read on the altimeter when the subscale is set to the standard pressure of 1013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg). It is used for performance chart calculations because all performance data is referenced to standard pressure.

questions.question: Density altitude is:-

options.text: pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature
indicated altitude corrected for instrument error
the same as pressure altitude in all conditions

questions.explanation: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature. It represents the altitude in the standard atmosphere at which the actual air density would be found. Higher temperatures increase density altitude, reducing helicopter performance.

questions.question: Airfield elevation 5000 ft, QNH 1003. The pressure altitude is:-
Airfield elevation 3500 ft, QNH 1023. The pressure altitude is:-
The ISA temperature at sea level is:-
questions.explanation: The International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) defines the sea level temperature as +15°C (59°F), with a pressure of 1013.25 hPa. Temperature decreases at approximately 2°C per 1000 ft (or 1.98°C per 1000 ft more precisely).

questions.question: The ISA temperature lapse rate in the troposphere is approximately:-
questions.explanation: In the ISA, temperature decreases at approximately 2°C per 1000 ft (1.98°C/1000 ft or 6.5°C/km) from sea level up to the tropopause at 36,090 ft. This lapse rate is used to calculate ISA temperatures at any altitude.

questions.question: The ISA temperature at 5000 ft pressure altitude is:-
questions.explanation: ISA temperature at altitude = 15 - (2 × altitude in thousands) = 15 - (2 × 5) = 15 - 10 = +5°C.

questions.question: If the temperature at pressure altitude 4000 ft is ISA +10°C, the outside air temperature is:-
questions.explanation: ISA at 4000 ft = 15 - (2 × 4) = 15 - 8 = +7°C. ISA +10 means the actual temperature is 10°C warmer: 7 + 10 = +17°C.

questions.question: 1 US Gallon is equivalent to approximately:-
questions.explanation: 1 US Gallon = 3.785 litres. Note that 1 Imperial Gallon = 4.546 litres. The US Gallon is smaller than the Imperial Gallon. This conversion is essential for helicopter fuel calculations.

questions.question: 1 US Gallon of water weighs approximately:-
questions.explanation: 1 US Gallon of water weighs approximately 8.345 lbs (3.785 kg). The weight of fuel per USG is found by multiplying 8.345 by the specific gravity (SG) of the fuel. For example, AVGAS with SG 0.72 weighs 8.345 × 0.72 = 6.0 lbs/USG.

questions.question: A helicopter has a fuel capacity of 50 USG. With a fuel flow of 8 USG/hr and a 45-minute reserve requirement, the maximum flight time available is:-
questions.explanation: Reserve fuel = 8 × 0.75 = 6 USG. Usable fuel for flight = 50 - 6 = 44 USG. Maximum flight time = 44 / 8 = 5.5 hours = 5 hours 30 minutes.

questions.question: A helicopter has a groundspeed of 110 kts and a fuel flow of 9 USG/hr. The specific range is:-
questions.explanation: Specific range = groundspeed / fuel flow = 110 / 9 = 12.2 nm/USG. This tells you how far the helicopter travels per unit of fuel consumed.

questions.question: A helicopter needs to fly 250 nm. Groundspeed is 105 kts, fuel flow is 8.5 USG/hr. The fuel required (excluding reserves) is:-
questions.explanation: Time = distance / groundspeed = 250 / 105 = 2.381 hours. Fuel required = time × fuel flow = 2.381 × 8.5 = 20.2 USG.

questions.question: The effect of a headwind on a helicopter's range is:-

options.text: range increases only at high altitude

questions.explanation: A headwind reduces groundspeed while fuel flow remains approximately the same. Since range depends on groundspeed (not TAS), a headwind reduces the distance the helicopter can cover on a given amount of fuel, thereby decreasing range.

questions.question: The effect of a tailwind on a helicopter's range is:-
questions.explanation: A tailwind increases groundspeed while fuel flow remains approximately the same. Since range depends on groundspeed, a tailwind increases the distance the helicopter can cover on a given amount of fuel, thereby increasing range.

questions.question: The effect of a headwind on a helicopter's endurance is:-
questions.explanation: Endurance is the time a helicopter can remain airborne on a given fuel load. It depends on fuel flow rate, not groundspeed. Since a headwind does not significantly change the power required (and therefore fuel flow) at the same TAS, endurance is essentially unaffected by wind.

questions.question: During the approach to land, a helicopter encounters a sudden increase in tailwind. The helicopter:-

options.text: will experience a loss of airspeed and tend to undershoot
will experience an increase in airspeed and tend to overshoot

questions.explanation: A sudden increase in tailwind (wind shear) causes a temporary loss of airspeed and lift. The helicopter will sink below its intended approach path and tend to undershoot the landing point. The pilot must add power to compensate.

questions.question: During the approach to land, a helicopter encounters a sudden increase in headwind. The helicopter:-

options.text: will experience an increase in airspeed and tend to overshoot
will experience a loss of airspeed and tend to undershoot

questions.explanation: A sudden increase in headwind causes a temporary increase in airspeed and lift. The helicopter will rise above its intended approach path and tend to overshoot the landing point. The pilot should reduce power to maintain the correct approach path.

questions.question: Wake turbulence vortices from a helicopter are most severe when the helicopter is:-

options.text: heavy, slow, and in clean configuration
light, fast, and in clean configuration
heavy, fast, and in dirty configuration
light, slow, and in dirty configuration

questions.explanation: Wake turbulence vortices are strongest when the generating aircraft is heavy (maximum lift), slow (high angle of attack/blade angle), and clean (no drag devices). These conditions produce the strongest tip vortices from the rotor blades.

questions.question: The maximum allowable weight (MAUW) of a helicopter is:-

options.text: the maximum weight at which the helicopter is permitted to fly as specified in the flight manual
the weight of the helicopter with full fuel and no passengers
the basic empty weight plus maximum fuel
the weight at which the helicopter can hover IGE

questions.explanation: The Maximum Allowable Weight (MAUW), also called Maximum All-Up Weight or Maximum Takeoff Weight (MTOW), is the maximum weight at which the helicopter is certified to fly. It is a structural limit specified in the flight manual and must never be exceeded.

questions.question: The useful load of a helicopter is:-

options.text: the difference between the MAUW and the basic empty weight
the weight of passengers and baggage only
the basic empty weight minus the fuel weight

questions.explanation: Useful load = MAUW - Basic Empty Weight. It represents the total weight available for crew, passengers, baggage, and fuel. The pilot must distribute this useful load while keeping the CG within limits.

questions.question: A helicopter has a MAUW of 2200 lbs and a basic empty weight of 1400 lbs. The pilot weighs 180 lbs and 2 passengers weigh 160 lbs each. The maximum fuel load (in lbs) is:-
questions.explanation: Useful load = 2200 - 1400 = 800 lbs. Crew + passengers = 180 + 160 + 160 = 500 lbs. Maximum fuel = 800 - 500 = 300 lbs.

questions.question: Specific gravity (SG) of aviation fuel is defined as:-

options.text: the ratio of the density of the fuel to the density of water
the weight of fuel per litre
the volume of fuel per kilogram
the temperature at which fuel ignites

questions.explanation: Specific gravity is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water. For aviation fuel, SG is typically between 0.71 and 0.73. It is used to convert between fuel weight and volume: weight = volume × SG × density of water.

questions.question: 25 USG of fuel, SG 0.71. The weight of the fuel in lbs is:-
questions.explanation: Weight = volume × SG × weight of water per USG = 25 × 0.71 × 8.345 = 25 × 5.925 = 148 lbs.

questions.question: A helicopter has 40 USG of fuel on board. Fuel flow is 7.5 USG/hr. The reserve requirement is 30 minutes. The maximum flight time available is:-
questions.explanation: Reserve fuel = 7.5 × 0.5 = 3.75 USG. Usable fuel = 40 - 3.75 = 36.25 USG. Flight time = 36.25 / 7.5 = 4.833 hours = 4 hours 50 minutes.

questions.question: A helicopter flies 180 nm at a groundspeed of 90 kts, then 120 nm at a groundspeed of 100 kts. The total flight time is:-
questions.explanation: Leg 1: 180 / 90 = 2.0 hours. Leg 2: 120 / 100 = 1.2 hours. Total = 2.0 + 1.2 = 3.2 hours = 3 hours 12 minutes.

questions.question: The performance-limited take-off weight of a helicopter is:-

options.text: the maximum weight at which the helicopter can meet all required performance criteria for the conditions
the basic empty weight plus maximum fuel
determined only by the engine power available

questions.explanation: The performance-limited take-off weight may be less than the structural MAUW. It depends on conditions such as pressure altitude, temperature, and wind. On a hot, high day, the helicopter may not be able to hover or climb at MAUW, so the take-off weight must be reduced.

questions.question: An increase in pressure altitude will:-

options.text: decrease helicopter performance due to lower air density
only affect engine performance, not rotor performance

questions.explanation: Higher pressure altitude means lower atmospheric pressure and lower air density. This reduces both rotor efficiency (less lift per blade angle) and engine power output (less air for combustion), resulting in decreased overall helicopter performance.

questions.question: An increase in temperature above ISA will:-

options.text: decrease helicopter performance due to lower air density

questions.explanation: Higher than standard temperature reduces air density (hot air is less dense). This increases density altitude, reducing rotor lift capability and engine power output. The helicopter's hover ceiling, rate of climb, and payload capacity are all reduced.

questions.question: The effect of increased gross weight on a helicopter's hover ceiling is:-

options.text: the hover ceiling increases IGE but decreases OGE

questions.explanation: A heavier helicopter requires more rotor thrust to hover. At higher altitudes, the reduced air density limits the thrust the rotor can produce. Therefore, increasing gross weight reduces the maximum altitude at which the helicopter can hover — both IGE and OGE hover ceilings are reduced.

questions.question: The IGE hover ceiling is always:-

options.text: higher than the OGE hover ceiling for the same conditions
lower than the OGE hover ceiling
the same as the OGE hover ceiling
unrelated to the OGE hover ceiling

questions.explanation: Hovering in ground effect (IGE) requires less power than hovering out of ground effect (OGE) because the ground restricts the rotor downwash, reducing induced drag. Therefore, the IGE hover ceiling is always higher than the OGE hover ceiling for the same gross weight and conditions.

questions.question: A helicopter's rate of climb will decrease with:-

options.text: increased gross weight, increased density altitude, or decreased engine power
decreased gross weight and decreased altitude

questions.explanation: Rate of climb depends on excess power (power available minus power required). Increased gross weight increases power required. Increased density altitude reduces both power available and rotor efficiency. Decreased engine power directly reduces power available. All three reduce excess power and therefore rate of climb.

questions.question: The service ceiling of a helicopter is defined as the altitude at which the rate of climb reduces to:-
questions.explanation: The service ceiling is the altitude at which the helicopter can only achieve a rate of climb of 100 ft/min. The absolute ceiling is where the rate of climb is 0 ft/min. The service ceiling is a more practical limit as it represents the highest usable altitude.

questions.question: A helicopter loaded with a CG of 95.0" and weight 2000 lbs. 50 lbs of baggage is moved from the forward compartment (arm 70") to the rear compartment (arm 120"). The new CG is:-
questions.explanation: CG change = (weight moved × distance moved) / total weight = (50 × (120 - 70)) / 2000 = (50 × 50) / 2000 = 2500 / 2000 = 1.25". New CG = 95.0 + 1.25 = 96.25".

questions.question: 1 kilogram is equivalent to approximately:-
questions.explanation: 1 kilogram = 2.205 lbs (or approximately 2.2 lbs). Conversely, 1 lb = 0.4536 kg. This conversion is frequently needed in helicopter flight planning when working with both metric and imperial units.

questions.question: 1 Imperial Gallon is equivalent to approximately:-
questions.explanation: 1 Imperial Gallon = 4.546 litres. 1 US Gallon = 3.785 litres. The Imperial Gallon is larger than the US Gallon. When converting fuel quantities, it is essential to know which gallon unit is being used.

questions.question: A helicopter has a fuel flow of 35 litres/hr. The fuel flow in USG/hr is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Fuel flow in USG/hr = litres/hr ÷ 3.785 = 35 / 3.785 = 9.25 ≈ 9.2 USG/hr.

questions.question: The crosswind component for a wind of 30 kts at 45° to the runway is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Crosswind component = wind speed × sin(angle) = 30 × sin(45°) = 30 × 0.707 = 21.2 ≈ 21 kts.

questions.question: The headwind component for a wind of 30 kts at 45° to the runway is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Headwind component = wind speed × cos(angle) = 30 × cos(45°) = 30 × 0.707 = 21.2 ≈ 21 kts. At 45°, the headwind and crosswind components are equal.

questions.question: A helicopter departs with 45 USG of fuel. After flying for 2.5 hours at a fuel flow of 8 USG/hr, the remaining fuel is:-
questions.explanation: Fuel consumed = fuel flow × time = 8 × 2.5 = 20 USG. Remaining fuel = 45 - 20 = 25 USG.

questions.question: The point of no return (PNR) is the point beyond which:-

options.text: the helicopter cannot return to the departure point with the required fuel reserves
the helicopter must land at the nearest airfield
the helicopter has used half its fuel
the helicopter must declare an emergency

questions.explanation: The Point of No Return (PNR) is the furthest point along a route from which the helicopter can return to its departure point and arrive with the required fuel reserves. Beyond the PNR, the helicopter must continue to its destination or an alternate.

questions.question: When calculating mass and balance, if the CG falls outside the permitted envelope:-

options.text: the load must be rearranged or reduced until the CG is within limits
the flight may proceed with caution
the pilot should fly at a reduced speed
additional fuel should be added to correct the CG

questions.explanation: If the CG is outside the permitted envelope, the helicopter must NOT be flown. The load must be rearranged (moving items forward or aft) or reduced until the CG falls within the approved limits. Flying with an out-of-limits CG can result in loss of control.

questions.question: A helicopter has a TAS of 100 kts, a headwind of 15 kts, and a fuel flow of 8 USG/hr. The specific range (ground nm per USG) is:-
questions.explanation: Groundspeed = TAS - headwind = 100 - 15 = 85 kts. Specific range = groundspeed / fuel flow = 85 / 8 = 10.625 ≈ 10.6 nm/USG.

questions.question: The Vne of a helicopter typically:-

options.text: is only affected by gross weight

questions.explanation: Vne decreases with increasing density altitude because at higher density altitudes, the true airspeed for a given indicated airspeed is higher. This means the blade tips reach critical Mach numbers at lower indicated airspeeds, requiring a reduction in Vne to prevent compressibility effects and retreating blade stall.
